case: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever and peeling skin for 2 days. One week ago he had crusted lesions around the nose. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diffuse tender erythema with flaccid bullae over the neck, axillae, and groin. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin produces separation of the superficial epidermis. The conjunctivae and oral mucosa are clear. Leukocyte count is 16,800/mm3 (reference range 6,000 to 17,500/mm3). Culture of bulla fluid shows no growth; a nasal swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

questions.stem: A frozen section of the peeled skin is obtained and compared with a specimen from an adult with toxic epidermal necrolysis. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient's specimen?
options: Intraepidermal separation through the granular layer
Subepidermal separation with linear IgG at the dermoepidermal junction
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with separation below the basal layer
Suprabasal separation with rounded keratinocytes in the blister cavity
approach: Fix the cause: a toxin from a distant staphylococcal focus, not a drug reaction.
The toxin target sits high in the epidermis, so the split must be high as well.
Match the split level to the clinical picture: spared mucosa, skin that peels in sheets, and healing without scarring.
questions.why: Exfoliative toxins A and B cleave desmoglein 1, which holds keratinocytes together in the upper epidermis. The epidermis comes apart within the granular layer, so only a thin sheet of dead cells is lost and the living basal layer stays attached to the dermis. That is why the skin regrows in about a week without scarring. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is different in both cause and level: a drug-triggered cytotoxic T-cell attack kills keratinocytes through the full thickness of the epidermis, the plane of separation is below the basal layer, and the mouth, eyes, and genitals are usually eroded.
whyNot: Correct.
Linear IgG along the basement membrane is bullous pemphigoid, an autoantibody disease of older adults in which the blisters are tense rather than flaccid.
Full-thickness necrosis with separation below the basal layer describes toxic epidermal necrolysis, which would also involve his conjunctivae and mouth.
A suprabasal split with rounded, detached keratinocytes is pemphigus vulgaris, in which autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 cause painful oral erosions.

topics: Scalded skin syndrome versus toxic epidermal necrolysis
Epidermal split levels in blistering disease

questions.stem: His 6-year-old sister had a sore throat 2 weeks ago, followed by a diffuse rash with a rough sandpaper texture and then peeling of her fingertips. Which of the following additional findings would most strongly support scarlet fever as her diagnosis?
options: Vesicles on the palms and soles with oral ulcers
Crops of vesicles at different stages on the trunk
Flaccid bullae in the axillae with clear mucosae
Strawberry tongue with circumoral pallor
approach: List the childhood eruptions that end in desquamation, since peeling alone does not separate them.
Pair the preceding pharyngitis with the rash texture.
Pick the finding that belongs to streptococcal disease and to no other item on the list.
questions.why: Scarlet fever follows a group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin produces a fine, rough, sandpaper-like rash that blanches, along with a strawberry tongue from swollen papillae and a pale ring around the mouth known as circumoral pallor. Desquamation of the fingertips and toes comes a week or two later. Those mucosal and facial findings are the features that separate it from the other peeling eruptions of childhood, including her brother's toxin-mediated disease, in which the mucosae stay clear.
whyNot: Vesicles on the palms and soles with oral ulcers are hand-foot-and-mouth disease from coxsackievirus A, which does not follow a streptococcal sore throat.
Vesicles in several stages at once is the hallmark of varicella, and that rash itches and crusts rather than peeling in sheets.
Flaccid bullae with clear mucosae is her brother's presentation, caused by staphylococcal exfoliative toxin.
Correct.

questions.stem: His skin heals in 9 days without scarring because his basal keratinocytes stayed attached to the basement membrane. Which of the following junctional structures maintained that attachment?
options: Desmosomes containing desmoglein 3
Hemidesmosomes containing collagen XVII
Adherens junctions containing E-cadherin
Gap junctions containing connexin 26
approach: Name the structure that anchors the epidermis to the dermis, as opposed to the structures that hold keratinocytes to each other.
Note where the toxin acted: high in the epidermis, well above the basement membrane.
Reason from an intact basement membrane zone to rapid resurfacing without scar.
questions.why: Hemidesmosomes anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane using integrin alpha6 beta4, BP230, and collagen XVII, also called BP180. The exfoliative toxin never reaches them, so the dermoepidermal junction holds and the basal cells stay in place with their stem cell population. Those basal cells simply divide and rebuild the lost upper layers, which is why the skin recovers in about a week and leaves no scar. Scarring follows injuries that destroy the basement membrane zone and dermis, such as deep burns.
whyNot: Desmoglein 3 sits in desmosomes of the deeper epidermis and mucosa. It is the target in pemphigus vulgaris, not a structure that anchors epidermis to dermis.
Correct.
Adherens junctions use E-cadherin to link neighboring keratinocytes through actin, so they would not keep the epidermis attached to the dermis.
Gap junctions pass small molecules between cells; connexin 26 mutations cause keratoderma and deafness rather than loss of adhesion to the dermis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the bulla fluid shows no growth while the nasal swab grows Staphylococcus aureus?
options: Antibodies in blister fluid opsonized the organism before culture
The organism requires enriched media not used for blister fluid
Toxin from a distant site reached the skin through the blood
Bacteria in the blister were killed by neutrophil oxidative bursts
approach: Separate two ways bacteria damage skin: the organism grows in the tissue, or a toxin travels to it.
Use the culture results as the clue, since the organism is only at the nose.
Conclude that the blister is a site of toxin action, not of infection.
questions.why: Staphylococcus aureus colonizing the nose or an old impetigo site releases exfoliative toxin into the bloodstream, and the toxin then acts on skin far from the infection. The blister therefore contains toxin and separated keratinocytes but no bacteria, so its fluid is sterile. This is the pattern of toxin-mediated disease in general: superantigens such as TSST-1 and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins also act at a distance by crosslinking MHC class II with the T-cell receptor to cause widespread rash and shock. Cultures from a directly invaded lesion, such as a furuncle or cellulitis, do grow the organism.
whyNot: Opsonization marks organisms for phagocytes and would not keep viable bacteria from growing on culture media.
Staphylococcus aureus grows readily on routine blood agar, so media choice does not explain a sterile result.
Correct.
Neutrophils are sparse in these blisters, and a brisk neutrophil response is what fills a pustule or an abscess with organisms and debris.

dx: Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis complicating varicella
case: A 5-year-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the emergency department because of worsening thigh pain for 12 hours. She developed an itchy vesicular rash 4 days ago, and vesicles in several stages are present on her trunk and scalp. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 156/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. Her left thigh is swollen and dusky with poorly defined borders, and she screams when the skin is touched lightly. Serum creatine kinase is 980 U/L (reference range 30 to 150 U/L). Blood cultures grow group A Streptococcus. She is taken to the operating room, where the fascia is gray and separates easily from muscle, and necrotizing fasciitis is diagnosed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her pain is far out of proportion to the appearance of the overlying skin?
options: Mast cell degranulation in the superficial dermis
Reflex spasm of the quadriceps around the infected plane
Thrombosis of fascial vessels with ischemic injury to nerves
Stretching of the dermis by rapidly accumulating edema fluid
approach: Locate the infection: along fascia, beneath the skin that looks deceptively mild.
Name what the organism does there, which is to spread fast and clot off the vessels that cross the plane.
Connect that vascular damage to the nerves running with those vessels.
questions.why: In necrotizing fasciitis the organism spreads along the fascial plane and thromboses the small vessels that perforate it. The resulting ischemia injures the nerves traveling with those vessels, producing severe pain early, and it also cuts off the blood supply to the overlying skin, which is why the surface may look only dusky or mildly swollen while the deeper tissue is dying. Pain out of proportion to the findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, and crepitus are the warning signs that separate this from ordinary cellulitis, which stays within the dermis and subcutaneous fat. Later, as those nerves are destroyed, the area can become numb.
whyNot: Mast cell degranulation causes itching and wheals, as in urticaria, not deep unremitting pain with shock.
Muscle spasm may add discomfort but would not account for exquisite tenderness of the skin or for the gray fascia found at surgery.
Correct.
Edema alone, as in uncomplicated cellulitis or lymphedema, causes tightness and aching rather than pain of this severity.

questions.stem: Two classmates also have febrile rashes. One had 3 days of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis with white papules on the buccal mucosa, followed by a rash that began at the hairline and spread downward. Which of the following is the most likely cause of that classmate's illness?
options: Measles virus
Rubella virus
Human herpesvirus 6
Parvovirus B19
approach: Use the prodrome rather than the rash, since several exanthems look alike once the rash appears.
Read the enanthem: white papules on the buccal mucosa are Koplik spots.
Confirm with the direction of spread, from the head downward.
questions.why: Measles opens with a 3-day prodrome of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis plus Koplik spots, then a blanching maculopapular rash that starts at the hairline and moves down the body, often becoming confluent on the face. Rubella causes a milder rash with tender postauricular and occipital nodes and no Koplik spots. Roseola from human herpesvirus 6 gives several days of high fever in an infant that breaks just as a trunk-predominant rash appears. Erythema infectiosum from parvovirus B19 produces bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs.
whyNot: Correct.
Rubella would show postauricular lymphadenopathy with a brief, lighter rash and no Koplik spots or prominent cough.
Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola, in which the fever ends as the rash begins, and the respiratory prodrome is absent.
Parvovirus B19 causes slapped-cheek erythema and a lacy rash, without a catarrhal prodrome or oral lesions.

questions.stem: Thirty years later she develops grouped painful vesicles confined to a single thoracic dermatome. Which of the following best explains this distribution?
options: Hematogenous seeding of skin from a reactivated visceral focus
Local spread of virus through the epidermis from a single inoculation
Autoinoculation of virus into skin along a line of scratching
Reactivation in a sensory ganglion with transport down its axons
approach: Identify the eruption as zoster, the late sequel of childhood varicella.
Recall where the virus waited, which is the sensory ganglion.
Map the territory of one ganglion onto the skin to get a single dermatome.
questions.why: After varicella, the virus stays latent in dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia. When cell-mediated immunity falls with age or immunosuppression, it reactivates in one ganglion and travels down the sensory axons to the skin that ganglion supplies, so the vesicles stop at the edge of that dermatome and do not cross the midline. Pain often starts before the rash and can persist as postherpetic neuralgia. Reactivation in the geniculate ganglion gives Ramsay Hunt syndrome, with facial palsy and vesicles in the ear canal.
whyNot: Bloodborne spread gives a widely scattered rash, which is what happens in primary varicella or in disseminated zoster in an immunocompromised patient.
Spread through the epidermis from one point produces an expanding local lesion, as in molluscum contagiosum or a wart, not a band along a dermatome.
Scratching spreads lesions in a linear streak across dermatomes, which is seen with warts and molluscum.
Correct.

questions.stem: On arrival she is shivering and her hands and feet are cool and pale while her core temperature is rising. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Heat production exceeds a normal set point and dissipation has failed
Heat is being generated and retained to reach a raised set point
Peripheral vasoconstriction is lowering the hypothalamic set point
Skeletal muscle is producing heat independently of hypothalamic control
approach: Decide whether the hypothalamic set point has moved, which is what separates fever from hyperthermia.
Read the shivering and vasoconstriction as responses that conserve and make heat.
Infer that the body is defending a higher target, not failing to shed heat.
questions.why: Interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor alpha from the infection raise hypothalamic PGE2, which moves the thermoregulatory set point up. Until core temperature reaches that new target, the patient feels cold and responds with cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering, and piloerection, which is exactly the picture here. In hyperthermia, such as heat stroke, the set point is unchanged and the problem is heat gain or loss of heat dissipation, so the skin is hot and flushed and the patient does not shiver. That difference matters: antipyretics lower a raised set point and do nothing for hyperthermia, which needs external cooling.
whyNot: Heat production outstripping a normal set point describes hyperthermia, in which the skin is hot and flushed rather than cool and pale.
Correct.
Vasoconstriction is a response to the raised set point and does not change the set point itself.
Shivering here is driven by hypothalamic output; muscle heat production independent of the hypothalamus occurs in malignant hyperthermia.

case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an intensely itchy rash on her right foot for 10 days. She returned 2 weeks ago from a beach vacation in the Caribbean, where she walked barefoot and lay on the sand. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F). Physical examination shows a raised, serpiginous, erythematous track about 3 mm wide on the dorsum of the right foot that has advanced roughly 2 cm since yesterday, with excoriations alongside it. There is no regional lymphadenopathy. Eosinophils are 9% of leukocytes (reference range 1 to 4%). A biopsy specimen of the leading edge shows an eosinophil-rich infiltrate in the epidermis. The diagnosis is cutaneous larva migrans.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the responsible organism reached her skin?
options: A sandfly bite deposited promastigotes into the dermis
Larvae in feces-contaminated sand penetrated intact skin
A tick attached during several hours of exposure on the beach
Eggs swallowed from contaminated water hatched and migrated
approach: Match the exposure to a route: bare skin against warm, shaded sand.
Recall which skin parasites need a vector and which enter on their own.
Choose direct skin penetration by larvae from soil or sand.
questions.why: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the filariform larvae of dog and cat hookworms, usually Ancylostoma braziliense. Infected animals pass eggs in feces onto warm, moist sand or soil, the eggs hatch, and the larvae penetrate intact skin on contact, most often on the feet, buttocks, or thighs. The itchy serpiginous track marks their wandering. The other skin-presenting parasites and bacteria in this group need a vector: sandflies carry Leishmania, Ixodes ticks carry Borrelia burgdorferi with its expanding erythema migrans, and Dermacentor ticks carry Rickettsia rickettsii, whose rash starts on the wrists and ankles and spreads to the trunk, palms, and soles.
whyNot: Sandfly bites transmit Leishmania, which produces a papule that enlarges into a crusted ulcer at the bite site rather than a migrating track.
Correct.
Tick bites transmit Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which cause an expanding ring or a spreading maculopapular rash, not a 3 mm serpiginous line.
Swallowed eggs are the route for Ascaris and for Toxocara, whose larvae wander through the liver, lungs, and eyes in visceral larva migrans rather than tracking across the skin of the foot.

topics: Vectors and routes of skin infection

questions.stem: Her eruption remains superficial and resolves over several weeks without visceral disease. Which of the following best explains why the organism stays in this layer?
options: Eosinophil major basic protein confines the larvae to the epidermis
Sebum and surface lipids block movement into deeper tissue
The larvae cannot traverse the epidermal basement membrane
Keratinized squames are the only tissue the larvae can digest
approach: Walk the stages of a skin infection: entry through a breach, then invasion and spread to a given depth.
Ask what barrier sits at the bottom of the epidermis.
Tie the fact that humans are an accidental host to the larva's inability to cross that barrier.
questions.why: Humans are an accidental host for animal hookworms. The larvae enter the skin but lack the enzymes needed to breach the epidermal basement membrane, so they cannot reach dermal vessels and complete the migration to the lungs and gut that they would in a dog or cat. They crawl within the epidermis instead, tracing the visible track, and die after days to weeks, which makes the disease self-limited. Depth is what determines the clinical picture in skin infection generally: superficial epidermis in impetigo, dermis in erysipelas, subcutaneous tissue in cellulitis, and fascia in necrotizing fasciitis.
whyNot: Eosinophils gather around the larvae and cause itching but do not form the barrier that limits their depth.
Surface lipids and sebum slow some microbes at the surface, yet these larvae have already passed through the stratum corneum.
Correct.
The larvae feed on epidermal tissue and fluid rather than digesting keratin, and a diet restricted to keratin describes dermatophytes in tinea.

questions.stem: Six weeks after the track resolves, a brown line remains where it ran. Which of the following best explains this discoloration?
options: Transfer of additional melanosomes to keratinocytes
Proliferation of melanocytes within the basal layer
Hemosiderin left in the dermis by extravasated erythrocytes
Carotenoid pigment retained in a thickened stratum corneum
approach: Place the pigment: brown, in the path of a healed inflammatory lesion.
Recall which epidermal cell makes melanin and what it does with it.
Separate more pigment delivered to keratinocytes from more pigment cells.
questions.why: Melanocytes sit in the basal layer, derive from neural crest, and package melanin into melanosomes that they hand off through their dendrites to surrounding keratinocytes. Inflammation stimulates that production and transfer, so each keratinocyte carries more pigment and the healed area looks brown. The number of melanocytes does not change, and as the pigmented keratinocytes move up and shed, the color fades over months. The other two epidermal cells have different jobs: Langerhans cells come from bone marrow, carry CD1a and Birbeck granules, and present antigen, while Merkel cells in the basal layer serve light touch.
whyNot: Correct.
Melanocyte proliferation produces a nevus or a lentigo, which is a discrete lesion rather than a line tracing an old inflammatory track.
Hemosiderin deposition follows bleeding into the dermis and leaves a rusty brown color, as in stasis dermatitis or pigmented purpura.
Carotenoids tint the palms and soles yellow-orange in carotenemia and do not deposit along a healed track.

questions.stem: The biopsy specimen shows intercellular edema widening the spaces between keratinocytes, with eosinophils between them. The same epidermal change is the defining histologic feature of which of the following conditions?
options: Psoriasis vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris
Actinic keratosis
Contact dermatitis
approach: Read what the specimen describes: fluid between living keratinocytes, which is spongiosis.
Recall which group of skin diseases is defined by spongiosis.
Rule out the conditions defined by a different epidermal change.
questions.why: Spongiosis is edema between keratinocytes that pulls the cells apart and makes the epidermis look like a sponge. It is the defining change of eczematous dermatitis, which includes allergic and irritant contact dermatitis and atopic dermatitis. When eosinophils fill the widened spaces, the pattern is called eosinophilic spongiosis, seen with arthropod bites and other parasites, allergic contact dermatitis, and early autoimmune blistering disease. Each of the other conditions has its own signature: parakeratosis and acanthosis in psoriasis, acantholysis in pemphigus, and dyskeratosis with atypical basal cells in actinic keratosis.
whyNot: Psoriasis is defined by parakeratosis (nuclei retained in the stratum corneum) and regular acanthosis, with neutrophils rather than eosinophils collecting in the epidermis.
Pemphigus vulgaris is defined by acantholysis, in which desmosomes break and keratinocytes round up above the basal layer.
Actinic keratosis is defined by dyskeratosis and atypical keratinocytes in the lower epidermis from chronic sun damage.
Correct.

case: A 47-year-old man who sorts imported wool and animal hides comes to the physician because of a sore on his right forearm for 6 days. It began as a small itchy bump, became a blister, and then dried into a black center. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 2 cm ulcer with a black eschar on the extensor forearm, ringed by small vesicles and marked nonpitting swelling that extends to the elbow. The lesion is not painful. Tender axillary nodes are present. Gram stain of vesicle fluid shows large gram-positive rods in chains. The diagnosis is cutaneous anthrax.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the marked swelling surrounding his ulcer?
options: Capsular polypeptide blocking opsonization by complement
Lethal factor cleaving mitogen-activated protein kinase kinases
Protective antigen forming pores in the host cell membrane
Edema factor raising intracellular cAMP in host cells
approach: List the parts of the anthrax toxin and what each one does.
Pick the finding to be explained, which is massive fluid accumulation in tissue.
Assign that finding to the subunit with adenylate cyclase activity.
questions.why: Bacillus anthracis makes a tripartite toxin. Protective antigen binds host cells and delivers the two enzymatic subunits inside. Edema factor is a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that drives intracellular cAMP up, which disturbs water and ion handling and produces the striking nonpitting edema around a cutaneous lesion. Lethal factor is a protease that cleaves MAP kinase kinases and kills macrophages, contributing to tissue necrosis and the black eschar. The poly-D-glutamate capsule is antiphagocytic. Loss of pain in the lesion is characteristic, so a painless ulcer with a black center and heavy edema in someone handling hides or wool should bring anthrax to mind.
whyNot: The capsule prevents phagocytosis and lets the organism survive, but it does not move fluid into tissue.
Lethal factor cleaves MAP kinase kinases and kills macrophages, which contributes to necrosis rather than to edema.
Protective antigen is the binding and translocation subunit, so by itself it has no enzymatic effect on fluid balance.
Correct.

questions.stem: A coworker was bitten by a spider in a storage shed. The bite became painful over several hours and developed a central necrotic ulcer over the next few days, and on the second day his urine turned dark. Which of the following venom components best explains both findings in the coworker?
options: Venom hyaluronidase spreading through connective tissue
Venom sphingomyelinase D damaging cell membranes
Venom phospholipase A2 triggering mast cell release
Venom metalloproteinase activating the clotting cascade
approach: Note that two tissues are affected: skin at the bite and circulating erythrocytes.
Look for one venom component whose substrate is present in both.
Pick the enzyme that attacks membrane sphingomyelin.
questions.why: Brown recluse venom contains sphingomyelinase D, which cleaves sphingomyelin in cell membranes. In the skin it injures endothelium and recruits neutrophils, so the bite becomes painful over hours and develops a sinking central ulcer with a surrounding pale and red zone over a few days. The same enzyme acts on erythrocyte membranes, which is why a small minority of patients have intravascular hemolysis with dark urine, anemia, and jaundice. That combination of local dermonecrosis plus hemolysis is what distinguishes it from the painless anthrax eschar, where the heavy edema and lack of pain are the clues.
whyNot: Hyaluronidase is a spreading factor present in many venoms and bacteria, and it does not lyse erythrocytes.
Correct.
Phospholipase A2 in hymenoptera venom drives pain and allergic reactions rather than a slowly enlarging necrotic ulcer with hemolysis.
Metalloproteinases in viper venom cause bleeding and coagulopathy, with bruising and oozing rather than a dry necrotic center.

questions.stem: After 2 days of poor oral intake, his blood urea nitrogen is 34 mg/dL (reference range 7 to 20 mg/dL) and his serum sodium is 140 mEq/L (reference range 136 to 145 mEq/L). Which of the following best explains why the rise in urea does not shrink his cells?
options: Urea is excluded by the membrane and raises tonicity
Urea is actively pumped out in exchange for sodium
Urea crosses the membrane and equilibrates across it
Urea is osmotically inactive once it is in the plasma
approach: Separate osmolarity, which counts all solutes, from tonicity, which counts only those that cannot cross the membrane.
Decide whether urea stays outside the cell.
Predict cell volume when a solute sits at the same concentration on both sides.
questions.why: Osmolarity counts every solute in a solution, while tonicity counts only the solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane and can therefore pull water. Urea moves across membranes readily through urea transporters and reaches nearly the same concentration inside the cell as outside, so it adds to measured osmolarity without creating a lasting osmotic gradient. That makes it an ineffective osmole, and a high blood urea nitrogen alone does not shrink cells. Sodium and mannitol are effective osmoles that stay outside, so raising them does pull water out of cells; infusing solute-free water or 5% dextrose does the opposite and makes cells swell.
whyNot: Urea is not excluded by the membrane, which is precisely why it fails to raise tonicity.
There is no sodium-for-urea exchange pump; urea moves by facilitated diffusion down its gradient.
Correct.
Urea is osmotically active and contributes to measured osmolarity; what it lacks is an effect on tonicity.

questions.stem: On day 10, after the eschar separates, a secondary bacterial infection forms a fluctuant collection at the site, and aspiration yields thick yellow material with abundant neutrophils. Which of the following patterns of necrosis is present in this collection?
options: Liquefactive necrosis
Caseous necrosis
Fat necrosis with saponification
Fibrinoid necrosis
approach: Identify the setting: a pus-filled pocket in skin with heavy neutrophils from a secondary infection.
Recall what neutrophil enzymes do to dead tissue.
Match that digestion to its named pattern.
questions.why: Neutrophils release lysosomal hydrolases that digest dead tissue into a thick fluid, so pus-forming bacterial infection and abscess produce liquefactive necrosis. The same pattern occurs in the brain after infarction, where tissue liquefies and leaves a cyst. Caseous necrosis is the crumbly, cheesy debris inside tuberculous and some fungal granulomas, where the dead tissue is walled off rather than digested to fluid. Fat necrosis follows release of pancreatic lipase in acute pancreatitis or trauma to breast fat, with chalky saponified fat. Fibrinoid necrosis is a microscopic change in vessel walls in vasculitis and malignant hypertension. Anthrax itself rarely makes pus, so a pus-filled pocket at the site points to a second bacterial infection.
whyNot: Correct.
Caseous necrosis would be expected in a tuberculous lesion, with granulomas and giant cells rather than a neutrophil-rich fluid collection.
Fat necrosis with saponification occurs in pancreatitis or injured adipose tissue and leaves chalky calcium deposits.
Fibrinoid necrosis is confined to vessel walls in immune complex vasculitis and does not form a fluctuant pocket.

case: A 36-year-old man who immigrated from India 3 years ago comes to the physician because of two patches on his skin that have grown slowly over 18 months. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). Physical examination shows two well-demarcated hypopigmented plaques with raised borders, one on the left elbow and one on the left buttock, each about 6 cm across. Both are dry and hairless, and pinprick and light touch are absent within them. The left ulnar nerve is thickened and tender at the elbow, with weakness of finger abduction. A skin biopsy specimen is obtained, and acid-fast staining shows no bacilli. The diagnosis is tuberculoid leprosy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the distribution of his skin lesions and nerve involvement?
options: The organism grows best at temperatures below core body temperature
The organism requires the lipid-rich sebaceous environment of those sites
The organism spreads only along superficial lymphatic channels
The organism needs the dense eccrine gland supply of those regions
approach: List where leprosy strikes: skin over the elbows, knees, and buttocks, ears, nose, and superficial nerves.
Ask what those sites share, which is being cooler than the core.
Connect that to the organism's growth requirements.
questions.why: Mycobacterium leprae grows best at about 27 to 30 °C (81 to 86 °F), well below core temperature, so it settles in cool tissue: skin over the elbows, knees, and buttocks, the earlobes and nose, the anterior eye, and superficial peripheral nerves such as the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Invasion of Schwann cells in those nerves explains the loss of sensation, dryness, and hair loss within a plaque, and thickened palpable nerves with weakness. The organism also cannot be grown on artificial media, which is why diagnosis rests on biopsy findings and on the pattern of disease, with experimental growth limited to the armadillo and mouse footpad.
whyNot: Correct.
A lipid-rich sebaceous environment favors Malassezia in seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor, not this organism.
Lymphatic spread would produce a line of nodules up the limb, as in sporotrichosis.
Eccrine gland density is highest on the palms and soles, which are not the sites most affected here.

questions.stem: The organism multiplies inside the Schwann cells of his ulnar nerve. Those cells share an embryonic origin with which of the following?
options: Skeletal muscle of the limb
Dermis of the lower back
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Type II pneumocytes of the lung alveolus
approach: Name the germ layer derivative that Schwann cells come from.
Scan the options for the other structure built from that same population.
Confirm the rest come from mesoderm or endoderm.
questions.why: Schwann cells arise from neural crest, the population that delaminates from the edges of the neural plate and migrates widely. Its other derivatives include melanocytes, dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, odontoblasts, and much of the facial skeleton and facial dermis. By contrast, limb muscle and the dermis of the back come from somites, and alveolar epithelium comes from endoderm. The split in dermal origin is worth holding onto: facial dermis is neural crest, while dermis of the trunk and back comes from the somite dermatome and dermis of the limbs from somatic mesoderm.
whyNot: Limb skeletal muscle comes from somites, specifically the myotome, and not from neural crest.
Dermis of the lower back arises from the somite dermatome, unlike facial dermis, which is neural crest.
Correct.
Type II pneumocytes arise from endoderm of the respiratory diverticulum.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most likely be present on closer examination of his biopsy specimen?
options: Central caseation within confluent granulomas
Noncaseating granulomas surrounding dermal nerves
Sheets of foamy macrophages filled with bacilli
Dense neutrophil collections destroying dermal nerves
approach: Decide which arm of the immune response is dominant, using the few bacilli and few well-defined lesions.
Recall what a strong cell-mediated response builds in tissue.
Check whether this granuloma type has central necrosis.
questions.why: A strong Th1 response with interferon-gamma activates macrophages, which organize into granulomas that wall off the organism. In tuberculoid leprosy those granulomas form around and within dermal nerves, they are noncaseating, and bacilli are scarce or absent on acid-fast staining, which fits his negative acid-fast stain and his small number of lesions. Caseation is typical of tuberculosis, where the center of the granuloma dies. Sarcoidosis is the other classic noncaseating pattern. The opposite pole of leprosy, lepromatous disease, reflects a weak cell-mediated response with a Th2 shift: macrophages are foamy and loaded with bacilli, lesions are diffuse nodules, and the face coarsens.
whyNot: Central caseation points to tuberculosis rather than to the tuberculoid pole of leprosy, where granulomas lack necrosis.
Correct.
Foamy macrophages packed with bacilli are the picture of lepromatous leprosy, which has diffuse nodules rather than two sharp plaques.
Neutrophil-rich destruction occurs in pyogenic infection and in erythema nodosum leprosum, not in a slowly enlarging anesthetic plaque.

questions.stem: His plaques no longer sweat, and the skin over them stays cool. In a cold room, which of the following mechanisms most directly limits heat loss from his skin?
options: Uncoupling protein 1 activity in brown adipose tissue
Rhythmic contraction of skeletal muscle during shivering
Sympathetic vasoconstriction of cutaneous arterioles
Thyroid hormone driving basal metabolic rate upward
approach: Separate two strategies in the cold: make more heat, or lose less of it.
The question asks about heat loss, so look at skin blood flow.
Choose the response that moves blood away from the surface.
questions.why: Heat leaves the body mostly from the skin, and the amount lost depends on how much warm blood reaches the surface. Sympathetic fibers constrict cutaneous arterioles and close arteriovenous anastomoses in the cold, which shifts blood to deeper vessels and cuts conductive and radiant loss directly. Shivering, nonshivering thermogenesis through uncoupling protein 1 in brown fat, and thyroid hormone all raise heat production instead, which is a separate strategy. Newborns rely on brown fat because they cannot shiver effectively. Damage to peripheral autonomic fibers in leprosy is also why his plaques do not sweat and the skin is dry.
whyNot: Uncoupling protein 1 generates heat in brown fat, which is production rather than reduced loss, and it matters most in neonates.
Shivering produces heat through muscle contraction and does not reduce loss from the skin.
Correct.
Thyroid hormone raises metabolic heat production over days to weeks and is not a mechanism for conserving heat.
